_note: Brightleaf Tea is made up. Every name, figure and source here is fiction, written to test the whiteboard.

company.name: Brightleaf Tea
company.line: Buys tea from growers, blends and packs it, and sells it in shops under its own brand.

maps.question: What does Brightleaf sell, and who buys it?
maps.summary: It sells packaged tea under one brand. Most of it goes to households through small shops, and a growing part goes to cafes and offices in bulk.

nodes.label: Everyday tea packs
nodes.sub: Loose tea and tea bags for the home
nodes.detail: The ordinary packs people buy for home. This is where most of the money comes from, and people buy them again every few weeks.

nodes.label: Premium blends
nodes.detail: Smaller packs sold at a higher price. Each one earns more than an everyday pack, but far fewer are sold.

nodes.label: Bulk tea for cafes
nodes.detail: Tea sold in big sacks to places that brew it for their own customers. It earns less per kilo but orders are large and steady.

nodes.label: Brightleaf Tea
nodes.detail: The company in the middle. It does not grow tea. It chooses and blends leaves, packs them, and puts its brand on them.

nodes.label: Distributors
nodes.sub: Local firms that deliver to small shops
nodes.detail: Middlemen who carry the packs from Brightleaf's warehouses to thousands of small shops, and take a cut for doing so.

nodes.label: Supermarket chains
nodes.detail: Big shops buy straight from Brightleaf. They order a lot at once, and push hard on price.

nodes.label: Direct sales team
nodes.detail: Brightleaf's own sales people, who visit cafes and offices and take their bulk orders.

nodes.label: Households
nodes.detail: Families who buy a pack every few weeks. Many stay with one brand for years, which is why the brand matters so much.

nodes.label: Cafes and offices
nodes.sub: Brew tea for their own customers and staff
nodes.detail: Businesses that brew tea by the pot. They care about steady supply and price more than the brand on the sack.

walkthrough.title: Start with the company
walkthrough.text: Brightleaf sits in the middle. It does not grow tea. Its job is to blend it, pack it and put a brand people trust on the box.

walkthrough.title: Three things on the shelf
walkthrough.text: It sells three kinds of tea. Everyday packs bring in about 71 of every 100 rupees. Premium blends and bulk sacks make up the rest.

walkthrough.title: Getting it to the shops
walkthrough.text: The tea reaches buyers three ways: through local distributors who serve small shops, straight to supermarket chains, and through its own sales team for bulk orders.

walkthrough.title: Who ends up buying
walkthrough.text: Most tea ends up in homes, where people buy the same brand again and again. Cafes and offices buy in bulk and care more about price.

walkthrough.title: What this means
walkthrough.text: The heart of this business is one path: everyday packs, through distributors, into homes. If that path weakens, the whole company feels it.

maps.question: For every 100 rupees of sales, where does the money go?
maps.summary: About 58 goes on buying tea and packing. After running costs and advertising, roughly 12 is left as profit before tax.

nodes.label: Everyday packs
nodes.detail: Money from ordinary home packs. By far the biggest stream.

nodes.label: Premium blends
nodes.detail: Money from higher-priced blends. Smaller, but each pack leaves more profit.

nodes.label: Bulk tea
nodes.detail: Money from sacks sold to cafes and offices. Steady, with thin profit.

nodes.label: Total sales
nodes.sub: Everything customers paid in the year
nodes.detail: All the money that came in from selling tea during the year, before any costs are taken off.

nodes.label: Buying tea and packing
nodes.detail: The biggest cost by far: the tea leaves themselves, plus boxes, bags and the work of packing. When tea prices rise, this grows.

nodes.label: Advertising
nodes.detail: Money spent keeping the brand in people's minds. Cutting it lifts profit this year and can hurt sales later.

nodes.label: Staff, transport and the rest
nodes.detail: Wages, lorries, warehouses, offices and what distributors keep. These rise slowly whether or not sales grow.

nodes.label: Profit before tax
nodes.detail: What is left once every cost is paid, before the government takes tax. This is what a year of selling tea actually earned.

nodes.label: Paid to shareholders
nodes.detail: The part of profit handed to the owners as dividends. Worked out from the dividend per share, so treat it as a rough figure.

walkthrough.title: Money comes in
walkthrough.text: Three streams add up to total sales. The thick line is everyday packs: 71 of every 100 rupees.

walkthrough.title: The biggest bite
walkthrough.text: More than half of it, 58 of every 100, goes straight back out to buy tea and pack it. This is the cost to watch.

walkthrough.title: Keeping the business running
walkthrough.text: Another 30 goes on advertising, wages, transport and the rest. These don't shrink much in a bad year.

walkthrough.title: What is left
walkthrough.text: That leaves about 12 of every 100 as profit before tax. A small rise in tea prices can eat a large part of it.

walkthrough.title: Where profit goes
walkthrough.text: Roughly 5 of every 100 is paid out to shareholders. The rest stays in the company. That payout figure is an estimate.

maps.question: What has to arrive, and from whom, before a pack reaches the shelf?
maps.summary: Tea comes from estates and auctions, is blended and packed at two plants, and travels through warehouses to shops. One auction region supplies most of the leaf.

nodes.label: Tea leaf
nodes.detail: Dried tea leaf, bought by the tonne. Its price changes with the weather and the harvest, and Brightleaf cannot control it.

nodes.label: Boxes and tea-bag paper
nodes.detail: Cartons, foil and the special paper used for tea bags. Cheap next to the tea itself, but a pack cannot ship without them.

nodes.label: Northern tea auctions
nodes.sub: Most of the leaf is bought here
nodes.detail: Open auctions where estates sell their leaf. Brightleaf buys most of its tea here, so a poor harvest in this one region hits it hard.

nodes.label: Contracted estates
nodes.detail: A handful of estates that sell straight to Brightleaf on yearly contracts. This steadies the price for part of its needs.

nodes.label: Packaging makers
nodes.detail: Several firms that print and supply cartons and paper. Easy to switch between, so not a worry.

nodes.label: Blending
nodes.sub: Mixing leaves so every pack tastes the same
nodes.detail: Tasters mix leaf from many lots so the tea tastes the same all year. This skill is a large part of what the brand is.

nodes.label: Two packing plants
nodes.sub: Where tea goes into bags and boxes
nodes.detail: Two factories do all the packing. If one stops, the other cannot cover the whole country for long.

nodes.label: Regional warehouses
nodes.detail: Stores around the country that hold packed tea close to the shops, so orders can be filled in a day or two.

nodes.label: Shops and cafes
nodes.detail: The last stop before the buyer: small shops, supermarkets and the cafes that take bulk tea.

walkthrough.title: It starts with the leaf
walkthrough.text: Two things must arrive: tea leaf and packaging. The leaf is what matters. It is most of the cost and its price moves with the harvest.

walkthrough.title: Where the leaf comes from
walkthrough.text: Most leaf is bought at auctions in one northern region. The rest comes from estates on fixed contracts, which smooths the price a little.

walkthrough.title: Inside the company
walkthrough.text: Tasters blend the leaf so each pack tastes the same, then two plants pack it. Two plants is not many: a stoppage at one is a real problem.

walkthrough.title: Out to the shops
walkthrough.text: Packed tea is trucked to regional warehouses and from there to shops and cafes, usually within a day or two of an order.

walkthrough.title: The weak point
walkthrough.text: The dashed blue line is the one to remember. Brightleaf depends on one auction region for most of its tea, and it has no say over the price there.

maps.question: What know-how makes it work, and how hard is it to copy?
maps.summary: Nothing here is high technology. The edge is blending skill and a fast ordering system for distributors. Both can be copied, but slowly.

nodes.label: Blending recipes and tasters
nodes.sub: Decades of practice, held by a small team
nodes.detail: A small group of expert tasters and the recipes they keep. This is craft more than technology, and it leaves with the people who hold it.

nodes.label: Fast tea-bag machines
nodes.sub: Bought from a machine maker abroad
nodes.detail: High-speed packing machines. Any rival with money can buy the same ones, so they give no lasting edge.

nodes.label: Ordering app for distributors
nodes.detail: A phone app distributors use to order and track deliveries. It makes Brightleaf easier to deal with than its rivals.

nodes.label: The same taste every time
nodes.detail: Because of the blending, a pack bought today tastes like one bought last year. That is why people stay with the brand.

nodes.label: Low cost per pack
nodes.detail: Fast machines keep the packing cost low. Useful, but rivals have this too.

nodes.label: Shops rarely run out
nodes.detail: The app tells Brightleaf what each area is selling, so warehouses can be restocked before shelves go empty.

nodes.label: The brand
nodes.detail: A name people trust for one steady taste. Everything else on this map exists to keep that trust.

nodes.label: Tasters could leave
nodes.detail: The blending skill sits with a few people. If they moved to a rival, some of the edge would go with them.

walkthrough.title: No secret machine
walkthrough.text: Brightleaf has three kinds of know-how: blending skill, fast packing machines and an ordering app. None of it is high technology.

walkthrough.title: What the skill buys
walkthrough.text: Blending is the important one. It is why the tea tastes the same year after year.

walkthrough.title: What the tools buy
walkthrough.text: The machines keep costs low, which rivals can match. The app keeps shelves full, which is harder to match quickly.

walkthrough.title: It all feeds the brand
walkthrough.text: Steady taste and full shelves are what make people trust the name. The brand is the real asset.

walkthrough.title: Where it is fragile
walkthrough.text: The skill lives in a few people. If they left, the taste could drift, and the brand with it.

maps.question: Who else wants the same buyers, and what keeps them out?
maps.summary: Two large national brands and cheap local tea fight for the same shelf. Coffee and shop-brand tea pull buyers away. Habit and distribution reach protect Brightleaf.

nodes.label: Brightleaf Tea
nodes.detail: Brightleaf in the middle, with everyone who wants its buyers around it.

nodes.label: Crown Tea
nodes.detail: The biggest packaged tea brand. It spends far more on advertising and can afford to cut prices for longer.

nodes.label: Riverbank
nodes.detail: A national brand close to Brightleaf in size, and stronger than it in southern cities.

nodes.label: Unbranded loose tea
nodes.detail: Tea sold loose with no brand. It is cheaper, and it is what many buyers switch to when money is tight.

nodes.label: Supermarket own brands
nodes.detail: Chains selling tea under their own name, on the best shelf, at a lower price.

nodes.label: Coffee
nodes.group: Other ways to do the job
nodes.detail: Younger city buyers are drinking more coffee. It does not replace tea at home yet, but it takes some of the growth.

nodes.label: Buyers' habit
nodes.detail: People who like a tea's taste rarely switch. This keeps sales steady even when rivals advertise heavily.

nodes.label: Reach into small shops
nodes.detail: Brightleaf's distributors reach small shops that newer brands cannot get to cheaply.

walkthrough.title: Brightleaf in the middle
walkthrough.text: Everything around the centre wants the same buyers, or helps Brightleaf keep them.

walkthrough.title: The direct rivals
walkthrough.text: Two national brands fight it head on, and cheap loose tea undercuts all three. Crown is the one with the deepest pockets.

walkthrough.title: Pressure from the sides
walkthrough.text: Supermarkets now sell their own tea, and coffee is winning younger buyers. Neither is a crisis yet. Both are growing.

walkthrough.title: What holds the line
walkthrough.text: Two things protect Brightleaf: people stick with a taste they like, and its packs reach small shops others struggle to serve.

maps.question: What would have to be true for this to be a good business to own, and what would break it?
maps.summary: The case rests on buyers staying loyal while tea costs stay manageable. It breaks if leaf prices jump and Brightleaf cannot raise its own prices.

nodes.label: Steady brand, slowly rising profit
nodes.detail: The idea in one line: people keep buying the same tea, so sales are steady, and profit can grow slowly if costs behave. This is a way to think about the company, not advice.

nodes.label: Buyers stay loyal
nodes.detail: The whole idea needs people to keep choosing Brightleaf over cheaper tea and shop brands.

nodes.label: Can raise prices when tea costs more
nodes.detail: Tea leaf is most of the cost. For profit to hold, Brightleaf has to be able to pass higher leaf prices on to buyers.

nodes.label: Premium blends keep growing
nodes.detail: Profit grows fastest if more sales come from higher-priced blends.

nodes.label: Most sales are repeat buying
nodes.detail: The company reports that most of its packs are bought by households who bought the brand before.

nodes.label: A bad harvest lifts leaf prices
nodes.detail: Most leaf comes from one auction region. A poor season there raises costs for everyone, and the cheapest brands win buyers.

nodes.label: Shop brands take the shelf
nodes.detail: If supermarkets push their own tea harder, Brightleaf loses its best shelf space where city buyers shop.

nodes.label: Profit per 100 of sales
nodes.detail: Now about 12. If it falls for two or three reports in a row, costs are rising faster than Brightleaf can raise prices.

nodes.label: Share of sales from premium
nodes.detail: Now 17 of every 100. Rising means the growth idea is working. Flat means it is not.

walkthrough.title: The idea
walkthrough.text: Someone who owns this is betting on one thing: a trusted brand that sells steadily and earns a little more each year. This is a way to think, not advice.

walkthrough.title: Three things must hold
walkthrough.text: For that to work, buyers must stay loyal, Brightleaf must be able to raise prices when tea costs more, and premium blends must keep growing.

walkthrough.title: What supports it
walkthrough.text: The company says most of its sales are repeat buying. That is real support for loyalty.

walkthrough.title: What could break it
walkthrough.text: A bad harvest would test whether it can raise prices. Supermarket brands would test loyalty. Either could break the idea.

walkthrough.title: How you would know
walkthrough.text: Two numbers tell you which way it is going: profit per 100 of sales, and how much of sales is premium. Watch them each time results come out.
